newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - becalmed by year-end break.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - becalmed by year-end break.

text.p: European oil product prices will drift sideways this week as the continent closes shop for the Christmas break, traders said.
Next week should see an increase in activity, but most business is expected to start in earnest only from January 6. Much depends on the weather, a cold snap could herald a rush.
Gas oil, dumped in the doldrums by slack demand in the run-up to Christmas, is due for a very quiet holiday period.
But early January is more uncertain, with temperatures and demand hard to call. Forecasters at present see no severe cold and U.S. and Asia arbs could well provide the main action.

Traders say that, barring a very sharp cold snap, prompt cif NWE cargoes look set to continue at the equivalent to a premium of $4/5 to Jan IPE gas oil futures, mainly because the German inland market is relaxed despite historically low stocks.

Barges are set to hover around Jan IPE screen levels, possibly picking up $2 or so as Germany resumes regular buying in January. Low sulphur diesel cargoes and barges are seen languishing at Jan IPE +$13/16 and $9/13 into early January.
Naphtha markets are expecetd to remain muted over the next couple of weeks with little fresh buying interest from end-users and few aggresive sellers.

Despite the current overhang of prompt supply, traders saw relaxed petrochemical buying interest and prices holding in the current wide range - bids at $216-217 a tonne cif NWE with notional offers were around $220.

Cargoes of Egyptian and Algerian material, of 25-30,000 tonnes, were available around the end of the month. None have yet been offered into Europe and they may go transatlantic unless European demand picks up.
However, trades said that improved demand, particulary for lighter grades, in early January had boosted January swaps last week by around $4-5 a tonne.
Gasoline was seen holding steady, supported by good fob buying to build cargoes for arbitrage out of the region.
Some European inland demand was also anticipated, but most was expected to be met by local refiner and importer stocks.
Low sulphur cracked fuel is set for a quiet period this week but for marginally increased demand after Christmas.
"I would expect fuel to strengthen against crude (from current levels of $125 fob NWE) - its getting colder and U.S prices are fairly strong," said one trader at a major.
The main Med buyer will probably also look for second half January barrels.
But supplies may not be so thick on the ground following the 100,000 tonnes sold last week.
The high sulphur cracked market was expected to remain dead and prices may soften after Christmas.
"There's a number of cargoes around, I see at least three and not much demand and there's material coming from the U.S," said one trader, who added that the barge market looked full.
Prices may lose ground in an effort to kickstart buying interest. "We may see $100-105 fob NWE which should attract end-user buying, but then prices will recover," one dealer said.
